A B S T R A C T   
Malignant invasive Erigeron canadensis, as a typical lignocellulosic biomass, is a formidable challenge for sus­
tainable and efficient resource utilization, however nanobubble water (NBW) coupled with anaerobic digestion 
furnishes a prospective strategy with superior environmental and economic effectiveness. In this study, influence 
mechanism of various O2-NBW addition times on methanogenic performance of E. canadensis during anaerobic 
digestion were performed to achieve the optimal pollution-free energy conversion. Results showed that sup­
plementation of O2-NBW in digestion system could significantly enhance the methane production by 
10.70–16.17%, while the maximum cumulative methane production reached 343.18 mL g−1 VS in the case of 
one-time O2-NBW addition on day 0. Furthermore, addition of O2-NBW was conducive to an increase of 2–90% in 
the activities of dehydrogenase, α-glucosidase and coenzyme F420. Simultaneously, both facultative bacteria and 
methanogenic archaea were enriched as well, further indicating that O2-NBW might be responsible for facili­
tating hydrolytic acidification and methanogenesis. Based on Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) 
cluster analysis, provision of O2-NBW enhanced the metabolism of carbohydrate and amino acid, translation as

1. Introduction 
Vigorous development of renewable energy sources is a paramount 
strategy to achieve energy security and transition in diverse countries 
throughout the world, while making contributions to alleviating the 
tension on fossil fuels as well as coping with the challenges of global 
climate change (Bian et al., 2021). One of the foremost renewable en­
ergy sources, in a long-term perspective, is biomass resource, because of 
its substantial richness, variety of transformations and great significance 
to carbon neutrality (World Bioenergy Association, 2021). Driven by 
this circumstance, invasive alien plants such as horseweed (Erigeron 
canadensis), water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes), alligator weed 
(Alternanthera philoxeroides) and cordgrass (Spartina alterniflora), as 
promising biomass resources due to their low cost and tremendous re­
serves, offer excellent occasions for the sustainable conversion of energy 
(Li et al., 2020). 
Erigeron canadensis, popularly known as horseweed, is a fleetly 
colonizing invasive annual weed worldwide, especially in China and 
Europe where it has been named as a critical weed for management and 
control (Galkina and Vinogradova, 2020). Originally from North 
America, however, this notorious weed spreads at a swifter speed via 
more prolific achenes (over 200,000 per plant) on account of stronger 
fecundity (Bhattacharya et al., 2022), in addition to be characterized by 
a briefer growth cycle and higher niche breadth. Moreover, the invasive 
E. canadensis can supersede native biota to occupy a dominant position 
within terrestrial ecosystems, including cultivated lands, pastures, hill­
sides, wildernesses, and river valleys. Detrimentally, invasion of 
E. canadensis is accompanied by the breeding of pests as a host, the loss 
of biodiversity due to secretion of allelochemicals (e.g., polyphenols, 
terpenoids and flavonoids), and the significant decline in the yield of 
staple crops (e.g., corn, cotton, soybean, sugarbeet, etc.) of around 
28–83% (Weaver, 2001). At present, the control strategies involved in 
E. canadensis are either unsustainable chemical measures like herbicides 
application, not economical physical measures like manual digging, or 
prolonged biological measures like obligate predators import, however, 
the net acreages encroached by its invasions continues to enlarge (Szabo 
et al., 2020). Hence, there is an urgent demand for sustainable inte­
grated management and efficient resource utilization of E. canadensis. 
With the advantage of being rich in cellulose but low in lignin con­
tents, E. canadensis is a powerful attractive candidate as a feedstock for 
anaerobic digestion. Furthermore, the anaerobic digestion treatment 
can not only accomplish low-cost and sustainable management of 
E. canadensis, but also attain the purpose of efficiently converting it into 
methane, an alternative renewable energy, which possesses superior 
environmental and economic effectiveness (Saha et al., 2020). Although 
the fast-growing E. canadensis is an ideal accessible lignocellulosic 
biomass for anaerobic digestion, a primary drawback is that the hy­
drolysis stage is rate-limited on account of its recalcitrant cell walls 
(Song et al., 2020). To overcome this obstacle, disparate strategies 
focused on enhancing methane production from anaerobic digestion, for 
example, pretreatments prior to digestion, improvements in configura­
tion of digesters, and dosing of diverse additives, have been attempted 
intensively (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2015; Guan et al., 2022; Haque 
et al., 2022). Nonetheless, the supernal energy and technology re­
quirements of above treatments, coupled with the potential for sec­
ondary pollution, are neither cost-effective nor eco-friendly. It is 
imperative to search for novel strategies to address clean transformation 
of bioenergy. 
Lately, NBW has drawn more and more attention as an additive with 
unique preponderance to advance the performance of anaerobic 
digestion of lignocellulosic biomass. Due to the enrichment of nano­
bubbles (NBs) with a diameter of less than 1000 nm in NBW, it is 
peculiar to greater specific surface area, faster mass transfer efficiency, 
longer residence time, higher surface charge, stronger gas solubility, 
more reactive oxygen species (ROS) and so on (Liu et al., 2016; 
Michailidi et al., 2020; Xiao and Xu, 2020). In the case of the primary 
forms of NBs in NBW, they are either surface bubbles that construct a 
gas-filled space at the interface of solid substrates, or free bubbles that 
undergo Brownian motion in the liquid phase (Theodorakis and Che, 
2019; Kim et al., 2020). Up to the present, with respect to a variety of 
NBs types in NBW, NBs of O2, Air, H2, N2, and CO2 have been studied to 
achieve high-efficiency promotion of methane production (Chuenchart 
et al., 2021). In the research by He et al. (2022), methane production, 
hemicellulose and cellulose degradation rates of corn straw were 
increased by 12–25%, 13–26% and 20–33% in digesters supplemented 
with NBW, respectively. In general, excessive introduction of O2 is 
deemed to have great negative impacts on anaerobic microorganisms. 
However, the addition of NBW containing O2 can achieve a delicate 
balance without generating over aeration or exceeding the antioxidant 
capacity of microorganisms (Wang et al., 2021). Strikingly, both 
Air-NBW and O2-NBW can create a microaerobic environment to 
tremendously accelerate the hydrolytic acidification stage of substrates, 
thereby boosting methane production (Wang et al., 2020b; Hou et al., 
2021). Compared with conventional microaeration technologies, 
O2-NBW is capable of persistently maintaining a microaerobic envi­
ronment via highly stable O2-NBs (Ebina et al., 2013). The prominent 
superiority of microaerobic environment is to heighten the diversity and 
metabolic activities of facultative bacteria that are involved in hydro­
lysis, and at the same time expedite the consumption of intermediates to 
stabilize anaerobic digestion system (Zhu et al., 2009). In addition, O2 
freed from O2-NBW zealously serves as an electron acceptor to motivate 
microbial activities by correspondingly accelerating electron transfer 
(Wang et al., 2020b). Nevertheless, a more in-depth study on the 
particular mechanism for O2-NBW provision to methanogenesis of 
complicated lignocellulosic biomass in anaerobic digestion system has 
not yet been fulfilled, in terms of disparate metabolic pathways of mi­
croorganisms, correlative enzyme activities, and carbon balance of the 
system. 
Therefore, this study investigated the influence of various O2-NBW 
addition times on methane production from E. canadensis which was 
firstly reported as the feedstock for anaerobic digestion. The prime 
purposes of this work are: (i) to monitor diverse conventional indicators 
of digestion system to explore the impact of O2-NBW addition on per­
formance of anaerobic digestion; (ii) to characterize the function of O2- 
NBW by measuring interrelated microbial enzyme activities; (iii) to 
expound underlying mechanisms based on exposure of bacterial and 
archaeal communities under O2-NBW provision; (iv) to assess carbon 
flow distribution in anaerobic digestion system supplemented with O2- 
NBW. To progress tenor of carbon-neutral vision, the results of this study 
are supposed to offer theoretical guidance and novel insights for effi­
cient recovery of energy from lignocellulosic biomass (E. canadensis) on 
account of O2-NBW adhibition in anaerobic digestion system. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Feedstock and inoculum 
E. canadensis was collected from abandoned farmland in Pen­
gjiazhuang Village, Weifang, Shandong, China. Before further treat­
ment, E. canadensis was dried, ground to pass through a 2 mm sieve and

stored in sealed plastic bag at 4 ◦C. Digested sludge was sampled from 
the Xianyang Road Wastewater Treatment Plant in Tianjin, China. The 
sludge was incubated at 35 ◦C for 2 weeks prior to employ to activate the 
microorganisms. At the beginning of incubation, the total solids (TS) and 
volatile solids (VS) contents of digested sludge were 4.84 wt% and 2.18 
wt%, respectively. Characteristics of feedstock (E. canadensis) and 
inoculum (sludge) are presented in Table S1. 
2.2. O2-NBW 
The O2-NBW used in this study was prepared by a NB generator (YC- 
MNB–III–0.15, Yuchuang Environmental Technology Co., Ltd., China) 
adopting a gas-water circulation method. O2 (purity ≥99.995%) was 
purchased from Tianjin Anxing Industrial Gas Sales Co., Ltd., China. 
Deionized water (DW) circulation flow rate, gas intake velocity and 
pressure of the NB generator were respectively controlled at 2.5 L min−1, 
0.07 L min−1 and 0.24 MPa for 20 min to obtain O2-NBW. In this 
experiment, the bubble concentration and average particle size of O2- 
NBs were 2.6 × 108 mL−1 and 189.4 nm, respectively. 
2.3. Experimental design 
4.5 g of E. canadensis and 200 mL of inoculum sludge (S/I = 4:3) were 
added to each 500 mL serum bottle, in which working volume was set as 
400 mL. In this study, both DW and O2-NBW total volumes were 
controlled at 150 mL for each digester. The different addition times were 
T0 (DW, on day 0, 150 mL each time, control group), T1 (O2-NBW, on 
day 0, 150 mL each time), T2 (O2-NBW, on day 0, on day 6, 75 mL each 
time), T3 (O2-NBW, on day 0, on day 6, on day 12, 50 mL each time), 
respectively. DW was exploited when adding O2-NBW on days 0, 6, and 
12 to ensure a consistent volume of liquid in each digester. To eliminate 
the biogas generated by the inoculum sludge, a blank with the same 
amount of sludge was added. Initial pH was adjusted to 7.20 with 2 M 
NaOH or HCl while an anaerobic environment was created by purging 
with nitrogen for 5 min. The experiments were carried out in a constant 
temperature incubator at 35 ◦C for 30 days with manual shaking once a 
day. Each group of experiments was terminated until the daily methane 
production remained less than 1% of the total methane production for 5 
consecutive days. All experiments were performed in triplicate. 
2.4. Analytical methods 
TS and VS were analyzed based on standard methods (Eaton et al., 
2005). Elemental composition (C, H, N and S) of feedstock and inoculum 
was analyzed by an elemental analyzer (Elementar Vario ELIII, Ger­
many). Lignin, cellulose and hemicellulose were determined by Van 
Soest method using a fiber analyzer (A2000I, ANKOM, USA). The pH of 
biogas slurry was measured by a pH meter (ST3100/F, Ohaus Starter, 
USA). The concentration of ammonia nitrogen was determined by 
Nessler’s reagent colorimetric method (HJ 535–2009, China). Biogas 
production was measured using a 60 mL syringe and then converted to 
volume at standard temperature and pressure (STP). Biogas composition 
(CH4 and CO2) was determined by a gas chromatograph (GC) (8860, 
Agilent, USA) packed with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) and an 
HQ + 5A column (50 ◦C), as well as the resulting chromatogram of 
which shown in Fig. S1. Injector and detector temperatures were set to 
80 ◦C and 250 ◦C, respectively. Helium as carrier gas was adjusted to a 
flow rate of 5 mL min−1. Liquid samples for analysis of volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs) were extracted via a 2.5 mL syringe, centrifuged for 5 min 
at 15,000 rpm and filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane. In order to 
acidify the filtrate, 20% (v/v) phosphoric acid (25% v/v) was added 
before being measured by a gas chromatograph (8860, Agilent, USA) 
equipped with DB-FATWAX UI column (30 m × 250 μm × 0.25 μm) and 
flame ionization detector (FID). Ingredients of VFAs in terms of acetic 
acid, propionic acid, isobutyric acid, butyric acid, isovaleric acid, and 
valeric acid were detected. The flow rate of N2 carrier gas was 
maintained at 25 mL min−1, while the temperatures of injector and 
detector were 250 ◦C and 300 ◦C, respectively. Two microbial enzymes 
(on day 6), including dehydrogenase (DHA) and α-glucosidase (α-GC), 
along with coenzyme F420 (on day 12), were assayed utilizing ELISA kit 
provided by Beijing ZKGX Research Institute of Chemical Technology, 
China.

2.7. Microbial community analysis 
Biogas slurry was collected for analysis of bacterial and archaeal 
communities after 30 days’ anaerobic digestion. After extracting mi­
crobial DNA, the V3–V4 regions of bacteria were amplified with primer 
sequences 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′) and 806R (5′-

sequencing library, and sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq platform 
(Illumina, San Diego, USA). Detailed steps were previously described 
(Song et al., 2021b). 
2.8. Statistical analysis 
In this work, all data were calculated employing Microsoft Office 
Excel 2019. The experimental data were expressed as mean ± standard 
deviation. SPSS 12.0 was used to conduct one-way analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) to analyze the significance of obtained results, and significant 
difference was assumed at p < 0.05. Origin 2021 was applied for all 
figures.

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Effect of O2-NBW addition on methane production from E. 
canadensis 
3.1.1. Daily and cumulative methane production 
Changes of daily and cumulative methane production along with 
associative methane content of E. canadensis during anaerobic digestion 
under different O2-NBW addition times are presented in Fig. 1. At least 
90% of general methane production was achieved within 20 days of 
initiation of anaerobic digestion. Over the digestion period of 30 days, 
the daily methane production of digesters with O2-NBW was higher than 
that of digesters with DW. As can be seen from Fig. 1(a), the maximum 
daily methane productions of T1, T2 and T3 with O2-NBW addition were 
36.79 ± 1.29 mL g−1 VS d−1, 36.08 ± 0.74 mL g−1 VS d−1 and 35.34 ±
1.89 mL g−1 VS d−1 on day 7, respectively, while that of T0 with DW 
addition was 34.12 ± 1.09 mL g−1 VS d−1. According to Fig. 1(c), the 
increase of methane content in the earlier stage was accompanied by the 
gradual increase of O2-NBW addition such as T1 with a 16.58% 
improvement in methane content compared to T0 during day 4 to day 6. 
Noteworthy, due to the addition of fresh O2-NBW on day 6, the methane 
content of T3 was higher than that of other digesters in the later stage, 
reaching as high as 69.46% on day 19. Thus, it is deduced that the 
presence of O2-NBW can promote higher methane content and better 
biogas quality, which is beneficial for energy recovery. 
As shown in Fig. 1(b), there was significant impact (p < 0.05) of O2- 
NBW addition of digesters to enhance cumulative methane production 
compared with DW addition. In this regard, compared to T0, the cu­
mulative methane production of T1, T2 and T3 groups were increased by 
16.17%, 10.70% and 13.30%, respectively. Similarly, Wang et al. 
(2020b) showed that an increase (29.9%) in cumulative methane pro­
duction from cellulose was obtained in the O2-NBW reactors. In addi­
tion, the maximum cumulative methane production of 343.18 ± 1.66 
mL g−1 VS was observed in T1 digester with one-time addition of 
O2-NBW only on day 0. Presumable reasons can be explained: (i) 
bursting of O2-NBs creates a microaerobic environment to strengthen 
the diversity and competence of facultative bacteria (as mentioned in 
3.4), thereby promoting feedstocks hydrolysis (Song et al., 2023), (ii) 
existence of O2-NBs with higher surface charge improves the efficiency 
of gas transfer as well as the activity of electron transport system (ETS) 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). In general, the anaerobic digestion system 
coupled with O2-NBW effectively achieved the maximum methane 
production of E. canadensis, however, the correlative mechanisms are 
necessary to further investigated. 
3.1.2. Kinetic analysis of methane production 
The fitting parameters based on the modified Gompertz model were 
listed in Table 1. The calculated P values were in good agreement with 
the experimental M(t) values, indicating that experimental methane 
productions were commendably fitted with the modified Gompertz 
model, with the supernal correlation coefficient (R2) greater than 0.996. 
T1 exhibited a remarkable rise in both maximum methane production 
and methane production rate, with the 16.77% and 11.50% higher value 
than T0, respectively. Moreover, the Rmax values were significantly 
different between the O2-NBW-added and DW-added digesters (p <
0.05), which further demonstrated that the addition of O2-NBW could be 
more conducive to methane production. However, O2-NBW supple­
mentation had no significant influence (p > 0.05) on the lag phase. 
On the basis of elemental analysis data and equations, the theoretical 
molecular formula and corresponding TMP of E. canadensis were 
calculated as C3.53H5.33O2.08 and 445.29 mL g−1 VS, respectively. After 
30 days of anaerobic digestion, the BD values (indicator for evaluating 
the degradation of organic matters) followed the descending order as T1 
> T3 > T2 > T0 (Table 1). The differences among the four groups might 
be attributed to the generation of ⋅OH from O2-NBs in the O2-NBW, 
which could be conducive to the breakage of C–C and C–O bonds within

3.2. Variation of O2-NBW addition on microbial enzyme activities 
α-Glucosidase (α-GC) is responsible for crushing α-1,4-glucosidic 
linkage to hydrolyze oligosaccharides and disaccharides (Gao et al., 
2020). Thus, α-GC, as a key enzyme straightforward determining the 
hydrolysis of primary organic fraction of E. canadensis, which is carbo­
hydrate, was selected to characterize the effect of O2-NBW on enzyme 
activity during anaerobic digestion. Seen from Fig. 2(a), the provision of 
O2-NBW improved α-GC activity to a certain extent, ranging from 1.53% 
to 8.36%. The results suggested that O2-NBW supplementation could 
enrich facultative bacteria (as noted in 3.4) and generate superior 
extracellular enzymes to expedite the hydrolysis, thereby offering 
abundant digestive substances for subsequent methanogens to indirectly 
boost methane production (Ruan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021). As an 
intracellular enzyme, dehydrogenase (DHA) is served as a measurement 
of electron transfer activity and holistic microbial activity during 
anaerobic digestion on account of its ability to catalyze dehydrogenation 
reactions (Wang et al., 2017). Notably, after O2-NBW addition, DHA 
activity in all digesters was significantly augmented (p < 0.05) 
compared to the control digester, confirming that the microbial activity 
was enhanced by O2-NBW. Specifically, the maximum DHA activity of 
220.84 ± 5.14 IU L−1 in T1 group is shown in Fig. 2(a), which was 
38.73% higher than that in T0 group. Therefore, a new strategy for 
achieving higher enzyme activities of anaerobic digestion system is to 
afford O2-NBW, thereby advancing methane production. 
Coenzyme F420, an electron transfer carrier peculiar to hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, is generally applied for revealing methano­
genic activity (Deng et al., 2021). The significant enhancement (p <
0.05) of coenzyme F420 activity during anaerobic digestion by the 
addition of O2-NBW is distinctly shown in Fig. 2(b), which was consis­
tent with the study by Fan et al. (2021b). On day 12, the activities of 
coenzyme F420 in T1, T2 and T3 were increased by 89.95%, 14.69%, and 
65.41% in comparison to the control group (T0), respectively. This 
indicated that O2-NBW supplementation could facilitate electron 
transfer in digestion system while enhancing the activity of hydro­
genotrophic methanogens, resulting in elevated methane production. 
Overall, the stimulation of O2-NBW on enzyme activities can accelerate 
not only hydrolysis but also methanogenesis, aiming to aggrandize the 
methane production from E. canadensis. 
3.3. Removal of VS, volatile fatty acids and pH during anaerobic 
digestion 
VS removal rate is supposed to display the hydrolysis and conversion 
efficiency of substrate in anaerobic digestion system. The changes of VS 
content and VS removal rate in various groups are shown in Fig. S2. 
Compared with T0 control group, the groups added with O2-NBW 
emerged a higher VS removal rate, of which the T1, T2 and T3 groups 
were 39.20%, 38.75% and 39.11%, respectively. Advancement of VS 
removal rate signified that the motivate effect of O2-NBW on anaerobic 
digestion of E. canadensis might be derived from the promotion of sub­
strate hydrolysis as well as achieving energy conversion efficiently. 
VFAs are intermediates generated after the hydrolytic and acido­
genic stages, which play a crucial role in the subsequent methanogenesis 
phase. Components of VFAs in term of acetic acid, propionic acid, iso­
butyric acid, butyric acid, isovaleric acid, and valeric acid are exhibited 
in Fig. 3. VFAs were abundantly inspired in all digesters after initiation 
of anaerobic digestion process, peaked at 4–6 days, and then leveled off 
after 15 days. Dissimilarly, higher VFAs concentration was manifested in 
the digesters supplemented with O2-NBW during the first 15 days, 
compared to the control group, which was statistically significant (p <
0.05). In particular, the O2-NBW groups aggrandized 38.41–56.99% 
more than the DW group in VFAs on day 6. Due to the presence of a small 
amount of oxygen, an increase in extracellular hydrolases manufacture 
from a more luxuriant community of hydrolytic bacteria can enhance

that the addition of O2-NBW might lead to faster not only production but 
also consumption of VFAs in hydrolytic acidification process, which in 
turn assisted in maximizing the subsequent methane production. 
Regardless of the digester, acetic acid, propionic acid and butyric 
acid were the predominant VFAs. Among them, acetic acid and butyric 
acid, which is a conversion source of acetic acid, positively contribute to 
methane production of methanogens (Komemoto et al., 2009). The 
concentrations of both acetic acid and butyric acid first increased and 
then decreased along with anaerobic digestion, and were lower than 80 
mg L−1 after 12 days. On day 6, acetic acid and butyric acid in the 
O2-NBW groups were 37.17–53.65% and 29.48–60.54% higher than 
those in the DW group, respectively. On the contrary, the accumulation 
of intractable propionic acid makes a negative impact on methane 
production (Wang et al., 2023). With the addition of O2-NBW in T1, T2 
and T3 groups, the percentage of propionic acid in the total VFAs 
dropped from 40.68% (T0 group) to 32.70%, 35.68% and 33.64%, 
respectively. In brief, the provision of O2-NBW was beneficial to the 
hydrolytic acidification of E. canadensis, which was consistent with the 
observations of α-glucosidase and VS as well. 
pH is an intuitive parameter to assess the stability of anaerobic 
digestion system, in relation to VFAs. In the early phase of digestion, the 
system pH declined unremittingly on account of the accumulation of 
VFAs, and dropped to the lowest value on day 5 (Fig. S3(a)). The lowest 
pH values attained in disparate groups were organized sequentially as 
T3 > T1 > T0 > T2. Moreover, the persistent period of lower pH coin­
cided with the period of higher VFAs. Subsequently, the pH value 
gradually raised and reverted to around 7.2. This might be caused by 
VFAs feeding methanogens for methanogenesis and the generation of 
ammonia nitrogen from proteolysis strengthening the buffering capacity 
of digestion system (Li et al., 2017). 
Ammonia nitrogen concentration is connected with the decomposi­
tion of organic proteins in E. canadensis. From Fig. S3(b), an initial in­
crease followed by a plateauing trend was shown for ammonia nitrogen 
in all digesters. On all accounts, since the concentration of ammonia 
nitrogen in all digesters were consistently less than 350 mg L−1 (<1000 
mg L−1 in the study of Fan et al. (2021a)), no ammonia inhibition 
occurred. 
3.4. Changes in microbial communities with O2-NBW addition 
3.4.1. Microbial community diversity 
Alpha diversity, including ACE, Chao1, Shannon, Simpson, and 
Coverage in this study, indicates the species richness and diversity of 
microbial communities. As shown in Table S2, high coverage (greater 
than 0.994) for both bacteria and archaea were presented, illustrating 
high representativeness and authenticity of the sequencing results. ACE 
and Chao1 indices were utilized to appraise species richness, while 
Shannon and Simpson indices were calculated to measure species di­
versity. The ACE, Chao1, and Shannon indices of not only bacteria but 
also archaea were significantly higher in digesters supplemented with 
O2-NBW, demonstrating that O2-NBW addition might fortify the rich­
ness and diversity of bacteria and archaea in digestion system, in simi­
larity with the observations of Wang et al. (2020a). The interpretation of 
this consequence could be that the microaerobic environment formed by 
O2-NBs blasting facilitates the growth and activities of fast-growing 
facultative bacteria (Guo et al., 2015), and in addition O2-NBW with 
stronger mobility of water molecules expedited the growth and meta­
bolism of more archaea. Furthermore, the more lively microbial meta­
bolism and complicated microbial community interactions, the greater 
contribution to methane production and conversion of organic compo­
nents. Hence, the particular mechanisms underlying involved in varia­
tion of microbial community structure by O2-NBW would be worthy of 
further investigation.

the acceleration of hydrolytic acidification of lignocellulosic biomass, as 
previously observed for enzyme activities and VFAs. Bacteroidetes is 
identified as proteolytic bacteria in charge of the hydrolysis of poly­
saccharides and proteins, while being strong oxygen-tolerant anaerobes 
(Vanwonterghem et al., 2014). A maximum relative abundance of Bac­
teroidetes was achieved in the T3 group (15.52%), followed by T1 
(13.85%), T2 (12.79%), T0 (12.15%) groups, respectively. Chloroflexi, 
as facultative anaerobes capable of decomposing cellulose, plays a 
crucial part in taking full advantage of carbohydrates (Serna-Garcia 
et al., 2020). The presence of Synergistetes is supposed to be inextricably 
linked with amino acid degradation, with emphasis on its synergistic 
oxidation function that mitigates the accumulation of refractory propi­
onate and butyrate, thereby enhancing digestive stability (Akyol et al., 
2019). Desulfobacteria is claimed to possess great metabolic potential to 
accelerate the utilization and transformation of nutrients (Cheng et al., 
2022). Thermotogae is able to fleetly make use of various mono­
saccharides such as glucose and polysaccharides such as xylan to 
maintain growth in a broad temperature range (Martinez et al., 2014). 
Collectively, the hydrolytic bacteria in O2-NBW digesters were enriched, 
especially facultative bacteria, implying the enhancement of hydrolysis 
during anaerobic digestion. 
In anaerobic systems, the presence and abundance of methanogenic 
archaea can make a direct difference to the velocity and efficiency of 
methane production. On the genus level, the dominant archaea found in 
this study were Methanosarcina, Methanobacterium, Methanoculleus, 
Methanomassiliicoccus and Methanosaeta, which were shown in Fig. 4(b). 
As seen, Methanosarcina (acetoclastic, hydrogenotrophic and mixo­
trophic), the most dominant archaeal genus, can flexibly utilize a variety 
of intermediates such as acetate, methylamine and methanol, as well as 
carbon dioxide and hydrogen to strengthen methane production 
(Ziganshina et al., 2022). Specifically, the relative abundance of Meth­
anosarcina was significantly enhanced in T1, T2 and T3 groups, ac­
counting for 85.15%, 79.10% and 81.96%, respectively, while it 
accounted for 75.30% in the control group (T0). In the work by Fu et al. 
(2016), the relative abundance of Methanosarcina doubled in optimal 
microaerobic conditions. Hence, it was deduced that the microaerobic 
environment constructed by O2-NBW supplementation could make a 
prominent contribution to the enrichment of oxytolerant methanogens, 
leading to an increase in methane. Moreover, hydrogenotrophic Meth­
anobacterium possesses the ability to expend hydrogen and carbon di­
oxide to generate methane, especially the performance of tolerance to 
restricted oxygen (Zitomer and Shrout, 1998). Apparently, the relative 
abundance of Methanobacterium in T1, T2 and T3 digesters with O2-NBW 
were 4.55%, 5.93%, and 5.55%, respectively, higher than that in T0 
(3.61%) digesters with DW. Similarly, it was reported that the relative 
abundance of Methanobacterium was as high as 10.1% after adding 
O2-NBW, compared with only 1.2% in the control group (Wang et al., 
2020b). As mentioned above, these findings further represented that the 
supply of O2-NBW showed positive benefits on the methanogenic pro­
cess. Methanoculleus, a hydrogenotrophic methanogen reported to 
augment in quantitative terms due to microaeration (Tang et al., 2004), 
was observed with the rise in relative abundance of 5.66–5.95% in the 
O2-NBW supplemented groups versus 4.40% in the control group. 
Hydrogenotrophic Methanomassiliicoccus is positively correlated with 
biogas production during anaerobic digestion and can establish a sym­
biotic relationship with sulfate-reducing bacteria producing hydrogen 
(Zhang et al., 2022), with the relative abundances as 2.55%, 3.04%, 
3.71%, and 4.98% in T0, T1, T2, and T3, respectively. Methanosaeta is a 
rigorous aceticlastic methanogen utilizing acetate as its sole energy 
source and own a higher affinity for acetate than Methanosarcina (Chen 
and He, 2015). Concretely, the relative abundance of Methanosaeta was 
elevated in O2-NBW digesters, possibly due to the more acetate pro­
duced by microorganisms prior to methanogenesis. Taken together, the 
archaeal community structure could be appropriately altered to achieve 
excellent performance of anaerobic digestion, with O2-NBW supple­
mentation, especially the enrichment of oxytolerant methanogens to 
guarantee admirable methanogenesis.

3.6. Preliminary analysis of interrelated mechanisms 
In accordance with research results, O2-NBW supplementation could 
achieve an increase in methane production. O2-NBW with O2-NBs has 
higher zeta potential, residence time, internal pressure and gas solubility 
than DW (Fan et al., 2020a, 2020b). Due to the disturbance of hydrogen 
bonding network of water via O2-NBs, the permeability of substrates 
into internal area of biofilms was enhanced, and hence the efficiency of 
mass transfer of nutrients and microbial activity during anaerobic 
digestion would be heightened by means of O2-NBW with strong 
mobility of water molecules (Wang et al., 2019). Bursting of O2-NBs as 
well as release of oxygen, interestingly, might create a microaerobic 
environment to reinforce the proliferation of facultative bacteria and 
activity of corresponding enzymes (Wang et al., 2020b), thereby facili­
tating the conversion of substrates in hydrolytic acidification process, 
especially accelerating the manufacture or consumption of in­
termediates such as VFAs. Additionally, there is a symbiotic synergy 
among diverse microbial groups during anaerobic digestion under 
microaerobic conditions, resulting in stronger stability (Fu et al., 2016). 
In particular, microorganisms in digestion system generally tend to form 
flocs in which strict anaerobes are surrounded by facultative bacteria 
(Liu et al., 2009). Facultative bacteria in outer layer can not only 
obliterate reactive oxygen species (ROS), but also deplete oxygen to 
decompose complicated organic substances into disparate in­
termediates, which are then utilized as substrates by methanogens 
(Stewart and Franklin, 2008). As a consequence, the amount of rema­
nent oxygen to the interior drops to the level within the tolerance limits 
of obligate anaerobic methanogens (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). 
Therefore, facultative bacteria are regard as both physical and biological 
barriers against oxygen in the outer layer, enabling the survival of strict 
anaerobic archaea and bacteria to perform their duties efficiently in a 
microaerobic environment (Botheju and Bakke, 2011). On the other 
hand, under oxidative stress conditions, a few strict anaerobes, such as 
Methanobrevibacter, Methanobacterium, and Methanosarcina, could 
manufacture antioxidative enzymes to acclimatize themselves to the 
oxidative environment, thereby enhancing their tolerance to oxygen 
(Brioukhanov and Netrusov, 2007; Horne and Lessner, 2013). Further­
more, O2-NBW could advance the ETS activity through the release of 
oxygen, as well as drive ATP synthesis in virtue of the TCA cycle (Wang 
et al., 2021). Last but not least, the addition of O2-NBW was beneficial to 
the enhancement of methanogen activity in the methanogenic phase to 
further boost methane production. 
4. Conclusions 
This study investigated the methanogenic performance of 
E. canadensis in anaerobic digestion system via diverse O2-NBW addition 
times. Supplementation of O2-NBW enhanced methane production by 
10.70–16.17%, while achieving the maximum cumulative methane 
production of 343.18 mL g−1 VS in the digester with one-time addition 
of O2-NBW on day 0. An increase in enzyme activities was observed in 
the O2-NBW digesters as well, about 2–90%, especially the activity of 
coenzyme F420 was significantly increased by 14.69–89.95% in com­
parison to the DW digester. Moreover, the addition of O2-NBW could 
advance the removal rate of VS as well as the generation and con­
sumption of VFAs in hydrolytic acidification process. An enrichment of 
not only hydrolytic bacteria (facultative bacteria) but also methano­
genic archaea (oxytolerant methanogens) was presented, which might 
be responsible for the accelerated hydrolysis and methanogenesis 
resulting from the addition of O2-NBW. According to KEGG analysis of 
bacterial and archaeal communities, the predominant functions 
augmented by O2-NBW supplementation were associated with carbo­
hydrate metabolism, amino acid metabolism, energy metabolism, 
translation, membrane transport, and cell motility. Last but not least, the 
provision of O2-NBW in the anaerobic digestion system achieved effi­
cient utilization of carbon in biomass based on carbon balance analysis.
